pos: n. (the third-named son of Noah, father of the northern and western peoples, and the man over whom the enlargement-blessing was spoken)
etymology: From Hebrew Yepheth, connected by Noah's own wordplay with pathah, to open wide or make room — hence “God shall enlarge Japheth”. The name is the blessing spoken in it.
biblical_def: Japheth is one of the three men through whom the whole present race of mankind descends. Moses is blunt about it: “These are the three sons of Noah: and of them was the whole earth overspread” (Gen 9:19). After the flood, when Noah lay uncovered in his tent, Japheth and Shem walked backward with a garment upon their shoulders and covered their father without looking on his shame, and the oracle that followed divided the post-flood world into three destinies. Ham's line through Canaan is put under servitude; Shem receives the LORD Himself as his God; and Japheth receives room: “God shall enlarge Japheth, and he shall dwell in the tents of Shem” (Gen 9:27). His sons are named in the first roll of the nations — Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech, and Tiras — and from them the isles of the Gentiles were divided in their lands (Gen 10:5). The northern and western peoples, the maritime and Greek-speaking world that the New Testament will later evangelize, stand in this column. And the enlargement clause is not merely territorial. To dwell in the tents of Shem is to be lodged inside the covenant household of another man's blessing, which is precisely what happens when the Gentiles are grafted into the olive tree and the middle wall of partition comes down.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Japheth; in sacred history he is a son of Noah, brother of Shem and Ham, and the progenitor of the northern and western nations.
webster_full: JAPHETH, n. A son of Noah, named with Shem and Ham, and the father of seven sons whose families peopled the isles of the Gentiles.
He covered his father with a garment, going backward, and saw not his father's nakedness.
Whence the blessing, God shall enlarge Japheth, and he shall dwell in the tents of Shem.
From his sons Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech and Tiras are derived the northern and western nations.
The name signifies enlargement, and is expounded in the blessing itself.
scriptures: Gen 5:32
And Noah was five hundred years old: and Noah begat Shem, Ham, and Japheth.
Gen 9:19
These are the three sons of Noah: and of them was the whole earth overspread.
Gen 9:27
God shall enlarge Japheth, and he shall dwell in the tents of Shem; and Canaan shall be his servant.
Gen 10:2
The sons of Japheth; Gomer, and Magog, and Madai, and Javan, and Tubal, and Meshech, and Tiras.
corruption_summary: The Noahic oracle has been abused for centuries as a charter for racial hierarchy, and is now dismissed as legend by the same handling that once weaponized it. Both readings ignore what the text actually says and to whom.
corruption_paragraphs: The oldest abuse of this passage is the reading that turned Noah's words into a permanent ranking of races — Japheth to rule, Shem to worship, Ham to serve. It cannot be got out of the text. The curse falls on Canaan by name, not on Ham and not on any modern people; it was discharged in the conquest of the land under Joshua; and the man on whom it fell has no descendants in any presently identifiable nation. Scripture's own summary of human origins forecloses the whole scheme: God “hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth” (Act 17:26). One blood. Every man in every column of Genesis 10 is a fallen son of Adam needing the same Redeemer, and the mercy that reaches him reaches him on the same terms.

The modern handling makes the opposite error and calls it progress. Because the passage was misused, the passage is discarded — the genealogy relabelled as an ancient ethnic charter with no historical purchase, Noah moved into the category of saga. The dictionary holds Noah historical, the flood worldwide, and the three sons the real fathers of the post-flood race, because the New Testament holds them so and reasons from them. And the honest answer to a text abused is the text read rightly, not the text dropped. Read rightly, Genesis 10 is the most anti-racist chapter in ancient literature: seventy nations, one father, one flood, one promise running toward the day when a multitude no man could number out of every kindred stands before the throne.
roots_summary: Hebrew Yepheth (H3315), Japheth; pathah (H6601), to make wide, enlarge; 'iy (H339), isle, coastland; Greek ethnos (G1484), nation.
roots_lines: Hebrew Yepheth (H3315) — Japheth; the name of Noah's son, tied by the blessing to enlargement.
Hebrew pathah (H6601) — to open wide, make room, enlarge; the verb behind “God shall enlarge”.
Hebrew 'ohel (H168) — tent; to dwell in another's tents is to be received into his household.
Hebrew 'iy (H339) — isle, coast, maritime region; the territory assigned to his sons in Gen 10:5.
Greek ethnos (G1484) — nation, Gentile people; the Septuagint and New Testament word for the peoples of this column.
usage: “God shall enlarge Japheth” — a name that is its own prophecy.
“He shall dwell in the tents of Shem” — room made for the Gentile inside a covenant not first his own.
“Of them was the whole earth overspread” — three men, one blood, every nation.

pos: n. (fourth son of Japheth; in prophetic usage the Greek world, Ionia and the seafaring west)
etymology: From Hebrew Yavan, the name behind Ionia — the Greek-speaking coastlands of Asia Minor and the Aegean. The Septuagint renders it Hellas, and the prophets use it for Greece.
biblical_def: Javan stands fourth among the sons of Japheth (Gen 10:2), and his own sons — Elishah, Tarshish, Kittim, Dodanim — spread out into the sea-lanes: “By these were the isles of the Gentiles divided in their lands” (Gen 10:5). What makes Javan more than a name in a list is what the prophets do with it. Ezekiel puts him in the great lament over Tyre as one of the merchant peoples: “Javan, Tubal, and Meshech, they were thy merchants: they traded the persons of men and vessels of brass in thy market” (Eze 27:13) — a trade in men, named as such, centuries before any modern conscience discovered the evil. Daniel sees the same people as an empire on the horizon, the rough goat from the west whose great horn is broken and replaced by four (Dan 8:21-22). And Isaiah, in the closing vision of the book, sends survivors of the LORD's judgment out to the far nations — “to Tubal, and Javan, to the isles afar off, that have not heard my fame” — that they may declare His glory among the Gentiles (Isa 66:19). The line runs straight from a genealogy to a missionary commission: the Greek world named in Genesis is the world Paul will walk, and the tongue of Javan is the tongue the New Testament is written in.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Javan; in sacred geography he is a son of Japheth and the head of the Ionian or Greek nations.
webster_full: JAVAN, n. The fourth son of Japheth, and father of the Ionian or Grecian people.
His sons were Elishah, Tarshish, Kittim and Dodanim, who peopled the isles and coasts of the Mediterranean.
The prophets use the name for Greece, and the Greek version renders it Hellas.
Javan is named among the merchants of Tyre, trading in men and vessels of brass.
In Daniel the kingdom of Javan is the Grecian empire that succeeded the Persian.
scriptures: Gen 10:2
The sons of Japheth; Gomer, and Magog, and Madai, and Javan, and Tubal, and Meshech, and Tiras.
Gen 10:4
And the sons of Javan; Elishah, and Tarshish, Kittim, and Dodanim.
Javan, Tubal, and Meshech, they were thy merchants: they traded the persons of men and vessels of brass in thy market.

And I will set a sign among them, and I will send those that escape of them unto the nations, to Tarshish, Pul, and Lud, that draw the bow, to Tubal, and Javan, to the isles afar off, that have not heard my fame, neither have seen my glory; and they shall declare my glory among the Gentiles.
corruption_summary: Daniel's Greek prophecy is routinely redated after the fact so that it predicts nothing, and Ezekiel's plain naming of a slave trade is passed over as though ancient traffic in persons were morally invisible.
corruption_paragraphs: Daniel 8 names the kingdom of Javan, describes its rise from the west, breaks its great horn at the height of its strength, and divides it four ways. Because that is what happened to Alexander, the standard critical move is to date the book after the events and call the prophecy a record. The dictionary rejects the redating and holds a sixth-century Daniel, for the plain reason that the book presents itself as prophecy and the Lord Jesus cites Daniel as a prophet (Mat 24:15). A method that converts every fulfilled prediction into late composition has not examined the evidence; it has adopted a rule that no prediction may be admitted, and then found what the rule requires.

The second corruption is a silence. Ezekiel says the merchants of Javan “traded the persons of men”, and it is common to read past that clause as commercial background. Scripture does not read past it. The Mosaic law made the stealing and selling of a man a capital crime — “he shall surely be put to death” (Exo 21:16) — and Paul places menstealers in the same list as murderers and perjurers as things contrary to sound doctrine (1Ti 1:10). The trade in image-bearers is named as sin by the God who made them, in the ancient world and in every world since; the honour of the prophets is that they wrote it down while it was still respectable.
roots_summary: Hebrew Yavan (H3120), Javan, Ionia, Greece; 'iy (H339), isle; rakal (H7402), to trade, traffick; Greek Hellas (G1671), Greece.
roots_lines: Hebrew Yavan (H3120) — Javan; the son of Japheth, and by extension Ionia and the Greek world.
Hebrew 'iy (H339) — isle, coastland; the habitat assigned to Javan's sons in Gen 10:5.
Hebrew rakal (H7402) — to travel for trade, to traffick; the merchant word of Eze 27.
Hebrew nephesh (H5315) — soul, person; “the persons of men” whom Javan sold.
Greek Hellas (G1671) — Greece; the Septuagint's rendering of Javan and the New Testament's name for the land.
usage: “The sons of Javan; Elishah, and Tarshish, Kittim, and Dodanim” — a genealogy that is also a map of the sea.
“They traded the persons of men” — the prophet names the traffic without euphemism.
“To Tubal, and Javan, to the isles afar off” — the Greek world marked for the gospel from Isaiah forward.

pos: n. (seventh and last-named son of Japheth, head of a nation the Bible names once and never follows)
etymology: From Hebrew Tiras, of uncertain derivation; the ancient association is with the Aegean sea-peoples. Scripture gives the name and no more, and the dictionary does not manufacture what the text withholds.
biblical_def: Tiras closes the roll of Japheth's sons: “Gomer, and Magog, and Madai, and Javan, and Tubal, and Meshech, and Tiras” (Gen 10:2), repeated word for word by the Chronicler a thousand years later (1Ch 1:5). That is the whole of him. No sons are listed, no land assigned, no prophecy spoken over him, no later mention anywhere in the canon. He is a man whose entire scriptural existence is a name in a column — and that is worth an entry, because it teaches something the fuller genealogies cannot. Genesis 10 is not a list of the peoples who would matter to Israel; it is a census of the whole post-flood race, and it includes the branches that leave no trace in the covenant narrative. The chapter's closing verse says so: “These are the families of the sons of Noah, after their generations, in their nations: and by these were the nations divided in the earth after the flood” (Gen 10:32). Tiras is counted there. The God who numbers the hairs of a head numbers the nations too, including the ones history forgets, and Paul will say that He determined “the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation” (Act 17:26) for every one of them — Tiras included, though no man now can point to the map and say where.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Tiras; in sacred history he is the seventh son of Japheth, named in the table of nations and nowhere else.
webster_full: TIRAS, n. The last named of the seven sons of Japheth.
He is mentioned in Genesis and repeated in the first book of Chronicles, in the same order.
No posterity, territory or history is assigned to him in the sacred text.
Ancient writers connected the name with the sea-faring peoples of the Aegean, but Scripture is silent.
The name stands as one of the seventy from whom the nations of the earth were divided after the flood.
scriptures: Gen 10:2
The sons of Japheth; Gomer, and Magog, and Madai, and Javan, and Tubal, and Meshech, and Tiras.
The sons of Japheth; Gomer, and Magog, and Madai, and Javan, and Tubal, and Meshech, and Tiras.
Gen 10:5
By these were the isles of the Gentiles divided in their lands; every one after his tongue, after their families, in their nations.
These are the families of the sons of Noah, after their generations, in their nations: and by these were the nations divided in the earth after the flood.
corruption_summary: A name with no attached history invites two opposite abuses — filling the silence with confident identifications the text does not support, or treating the silence as proof that the list is fiction.
corruption_paragraphs: The first abuse is speculative. Because Tiras is bare, writers have hung whole theories on him — this or that ancient sea-people, this or that modern nation, sometimes with prophetic charts attached. The dictionary declines. Scripture gives a name in a genealogy; where God has not spoken, confident speech is not faith but presumption, and the man who builds an end-times map on an unidentified son of Japheth has left the ground of revelation. Deuteronomy draws the line: “The secret things belong unto the LORD our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever” (Deu 29:29). Tiras belongs, for now, largely to the first clause.

The second abuse is dismissal. Because the name is untraceable, the whole table is filed as folk memory rather than record — a literary construct organized around the number seventy. But an invented list is exactly the thing that does not carry dead weight. A composer building a symbolic genealogy supplies each name with a function; a record preserves names whose bearers left no mark, because they were there. The Chronicler copies Tiras unchanged into a work written for a returned remnant with no conceivable interest in him, which is what men do with archives and not with allegories. The dictionary treats Genesis 10 as history because it reads like history at exactly the points where invention would have improved it.
roots_summary: Hebrew Tiras (H8494), Tiras; toledoth (H8435), generations, genealogical record; mishpachah (H4940), family, clan; goy (H1471), nation.
roots_lines: Hebrew Tiras (H8494) — Tiras; the seventh son of Japheth, of uncertain derivation.
Hebrew toledoth (H8435) — generations, begettings; the structural word that frames Genesis and marks its records as records.
Hebrew mishpachah (H4940) — family, clan; the unit by which Gen 10:32 divides the nations.
Hebrew goy (H1471) — nation, people; the seventy of Genesis 10 and the Gentiles of the prophets.
Hebrew 'iy (H339) — isle, coastland; the region assigned to the sons of Japheth.
usage: “And Meshech, and Tiras” — the last name in the column, and the last we hear of him.
“By these were the nations divided in the earth after the flood” — the untraceable branch is counted with the rest.
A name without a history is still a name God saw fit to preserve.

pos: n. (sixth son of Japheth; a northern trading people, paired always with Tubal, and named in Ezekiel's oracle against Gog)
etymology: From Hebrew Meshek, connected with a root meaning to draw or drag out. The Psalmist's spelling Mesech (Psa 120:5) is the same name; the KJV preserves the variation of its Hebrew text.
biblical_def: Meshech appears sixth among the sons of Japheth (Gen 10:2), and thereafter he never appears alone. In every prophetic mention he is bracketed with Tubal, as though the two peoples were a single northern fact. Ezekiel places them among the merchants of Tyre trading in slaves and bronze (Eze 27:13), lays them in the pit among the uncircumcised slain — “There is Meshech, Tubal, and all her multitude” (Eze 32:26) — and finally names them in the oracle against Gog: “set thy face against Gog, the land of Magog, the chief prince of Meshech and Tubal, and prophesy against him” (Eze 38:2). The Psalmist uses the name differently and unforgettably. “Woe is me, that I sojourn in Mesech, that I dwell in the tents of Kedar!” (Psa 120:5) — Meshech is far north and Kedar far south, and no man lives in both. The pilgrim is not giving an address. He is saying that a believer among the ungodly is a foreigner wherever he stands, hated for wanting peace: “I am for peace: but when I speak, they are for war” (Psa 120:7). That is the abiding use of the name. Meshech is the world a saint must live in and does not belong to.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Meshech; in sacred geography he is a son of Japheth and the head of a northern nation joined constantly with Tubal.
webster_full: MESHECH, n. The sixth son of Japheth, and the people descended from him.
In the prophets his name is always coupled with Tubal, as of two neighbouring northern nations.
They are named among the merchants of Tyre, trading in the persons of men and in vessels of brass.
Ezekiel joins them in the oracle against Gog of the land of Magog.
In the hundred and twentieth Psalm Mesech stands for a place of exile among the ungodly.
scriptures: Gen 10:2
The sons of Japheth; Gomer, and Magog, and Madai, and Javan, and Tubal, and Meshech, and Tiras.
Javan, Tubal, and Meshech, they were thy merchants: they traded the persons of men and vessels of brass in thy market.
Eze 38:2
Son of man, set thy face against Gog, the land of Magog, the chief prince of Meshech and Tubal, and prophesy against him,
Woe is me, that I sojourn in Mesech, that I dwell in the tents of Kedar!
corruption_summary: Meshech has been pressed into service as a cipher for Moscow in modern prophecy charts, on a resemblance of sound that the Hebrew does not carry and the passage does not need.
corruption_paragraphs: The best-known modern handling of this name identifies Meshech with Moscow and Tubal with Tobolsk, making Ezekiel 38 a prediction of a Russian invasion of Israel. The identification rests on nothing but the sound of the consonants to an English ear, and it has been repeated through a century of prophecy charts until it acquired the feel of a fact. The dictionary does not adopt it. Meshech and Tubal are named all through the Old Testament as trading peoples in the north of the world Israel knew; Ezekiel is not writing in cipher, and a reading that depends on the phonetics of a modern city name is a reading imposed on the text. Where the prophet is plain — that the proud northern coalition is drawn out by God Himself and destroyed on the mountains of Israel — the point stands without any of it.

Behind the particular error stands a general one: the habit of treating prophecy as a puzzle to be decoded from the newspaper rather than a word to be believed and obeyed. It thrives in the dispensational scheme, a nineteenth-century novelty that no Reformation confession knows, and it produces a reader more interested in the identity of Gog than in the holiness the oracle demands. Ezekiel states his own purpose four times over — that the nations, and Israel, shall know that He is the LORD. Peter draws the practical conclusion from the day of the Lord and it is not a map: “what manner of persons ought ye to be in all holy conversation and godliness” (2Pe 3:11).

roots_lines: Hebrew Meshek (H4902) — Meshech; the son of Japheth and the northern people named from him.
Hebrew mashak (H4900) — to draw or drag out; the root commonly connected with the name.
Hebrew gur (H1481) — to sojourn, to dwell as a resident alien; the verb of Psa 120:5.
Hebrew shalom (H7965) — peace, wholeness; what the psalmist is for while his neighbours are for war.
Hebrew Tuval (H8422) — Tubal; the brother-nation with which Meshech is always paired.
usage: “Woe is me, that I sojourn in Mesech” — not an address, a condition.
“The chief prince of Meshech and Tubal” — two names the prophets never separate.
“I am for peace: but when I speak, they are for war” — the sojourner's lot among the ungodly.

pos: n. (third son of Shem, born two years after the flood; the link in the line from Noah to Abraham and so to Christ)
etymology: From Hebrew 'Arpakshad, of disputed derivation; the Greek of Luke's genealogy renders it Arphaxad. The name's importance is positional, not etymological — it marks where the promised line runs.
biblical_def: Arphaxad is named third among the sons of Shem — “Elam, and Asshur, and Arphaxad, and Lud, and Aram” (Gen 10:22) — and he is the one the narrative follows. Genesis dates him with unusual precision: “Shem was an hundred years old, and begat Arphaxad two years after the flood” (Gen 11:10). He begat Salah, Salah begat Eber, and from Eber the line divides at Peleg and runs down through Serug, Nahor and Terah to Abram. Every covenant promise in Scripture travels through this man. That is why Luke, tracing the Lord Jesus backward past Abraham to Adam and to God, must pass through him by name: “which was the son of Arphaxad, which was the son of Sem, which was the son of Noe” (Luk 3:36). Nothing is recorded of his character, his works, or his death beyond the years. He built no altar, fought no battle, spoke no recorded word. He begat a son at thirty-five and lived four hundred and three years more (Gen 11:12-13). And that is the point of him: the covenant does not advance chiefly by heroism but by generation, by ordinary men fathering ordinary sons in the fear of God, until the fulness of the time is come. The genealogy is the thread on which the whole history hangs, and Arphaxad is a knot in it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Arphaxad; in sacred history he is the son of Shem, born two years after the flood, and an ancestor of Abraham and of Christ.
webster_full: ARPHAXAD, n. The third son of Shem, born two years after the deluge.
He begat Salah at the age of thirty and five years, and lived after that four hundred and three years.
From him descend Eber, Peleg, Serug, Nahor, Terah and Abraham.
His name occurs in the genealogy of our Lord as recorded by Luke.
Nothing further is related of him in the sacred history.
scriptures: The children of Shem; Elam, and Asshur, and Arphaxad, and Lud, and Aram.
These are the generations of Shem: Shem was an hundred years old, and begat Arphaxad two years after the flood:
And Arphaxad lived five and thirty years, and begat Salah:
Luk 3:36
Which was the son of Cainan, which was the son of Arphaxad, which was the son of Sem, which was the son of Noe, which was the son of Lamech,
corruption_summary: The patriarchal genealogies are treated as symbolic numerology rather than record, and the long lifespans are the pretext; but the New Testament reasons from these lists as history and hangs the incarnation on them.
corruption_paragraphs: The standard modern handling of Genesis 11 detaches the names from real time. The lifespans are said to be schematic, the numbers symbolic, the individuals representative of tribes rather than persons. Once that is granted, Arphaxad is not a man born two years after a flood but a literary counter. The dictionary does not grant it. Luke, writing careful history and saying so (Luk 1:3), puts Arphaxad in a chain of individual fathers and sons running unbroken from Adam to Jesus Christ, and a chain is worth nothing if some of its links are collective abstractions. Paul argues salvation itself from the historicity of one man's single act: “by one man's disobedience many were made sinners” (Rom 5:19). The genealogies are the connective tissue of that argument.

There is a quieter corruption in the way such names are handled devotionally — skipped. Readers pass over the begettings as filler between the stories. But Scripture is God-breathed in its lists as in its narratives, and the lists carry a doctrine the narratives assume: that God keeps covenant across centuries in which nothing dramatic is recorded, through men whose whole obedience was to marry, father children, and die in faith. Hebrews 11 ends by admitting that the faithful “received not the promise” in their own lifetimes (Heb 11:39). Arphaxad is one of them. The promise was four hundred years past his death and two thousand more past Abraham's, and it came.

Hebrew yalad (H3205) — to bear, beget, bring forth; the verb that carries the whole chapter.
Hebrew Shelach (H7974) — Salah, his son; the next link toward Eber and Abraham.
Hebrew toledoth (H8435) — generations; the heading under which Gen 11:10 places him.
Greek Arphaxad (G742) — the form of the name in Luke's genealogy of the Lord Jesus.
usage: “Begat Arphaxad two years after the flood” — the covenant line dated from the judgment.
“Which was the son of Arphaxad” — Luke will not skip a link between Christ and Adam.
A man remembered for nothing but fathering the next man in the promise.

pos: n. (son of Eber, in whose days the earth was divided; the name marks the generation of Babel)
etymology: From Hebrew Peleg, division, from palag, to split or divide. Moses supplies the meaning himself in the same breath as the name — the only son in the list whose naming is explained.
biblical_def: Peleg is the son of Eber and the brother of Joktan, and he is the one name in the post-flood genealogy that Moses pauses to explain: “And unto Eber were born two sons: the name of one was Peleg; for in his days was the earth divided” (Gen 10:25). The Chronicler repeats the note (1Ch 1:19), which means it was thought worth preserving through the exile and back. The division intended is almost certainly the scattering at Babel, recorded in the very next chapter: men of one language and one speech built a tower to make themselves a name, and “the LORD scattered them abroad from thence upon the face of all the earth: and they left off to build the city” (Gen 11:8). Genesis 10 lists the nations; Genesis 11 explains how they came to be nations. Peleg stands at the hinge. His own line is the plain one — he lived thirty years and begat Reu (Gen 11:18), and through Reu, Serug, Nahor and Terah the promise runs to Abram, so that the man named for the world's fracture is also the man through whom its healing is descended. That is the shape of the whole Bible in a single name: division comes by human pride, and the remedy comes by divine election running quietly through the same family in the same generation.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Peleg; in sacred history he is the son of Eber, so named because in his days the earth was divided.
webster_full: PELEG, n. The son of Eber and brother of Joktan, whose name signifies division.
He was so called because in his days the earth was divided among the nations.
He lived thirty years and begat Reu, and is an ancestor of Abraham.
The division intended is commonly understood of the dispersion at Babel.
His name is the only one in the post-diluvian genealogy whose reason is given in the text.
scriptures: And Eber lived four and thirty years, and begat Peleg:
And Peleg lived thirty years, and begat Reu:
Gen 11:1
And the whole earth was of one language, and of one speech.
Gen 11:8
So the LORD scattered them abroad from thence upon the face of all the earth: and they left off to build the city.
corruption_summary: The division in Peleg's days is regularly reassigned to continental drift or geological catastrophe, which makes a theological judgment into a physics event and loses the point Moses is making.
corruption_paragraphs: A popular reading takes “the earth was divided” as the splitting of the continents, and builds a rapid post-flood plate tectonics upon it. The dictionary does not follow. The Hebrew 'erets in this context regularly means the inhabited land and its peoples, and the immediately following chapter supplies the division Moses means without any need to look elsewhere: one speech became many, and the builders were scattered abroad upon the face of all the earth. Genesis 10 has already used the same frame three times over — the sons of Japheth, of Ham, of Shem, each “after their tongues, in their lands, after their nations” (Gen 10:31). The division is linguistic, national, and moral, and it is a judgment. Making it geological trades a doctrine for a mechanism.

The second corruption goes the other way, treating Babel as a myth explaining language diversity — a folk etiology of the kind found in every ancient culture. But Babel is not offered as an explanation of a curiosity; it is offered as an act of God against a specific human project, the attempt to build a name and a unity independent of Him. That project did not end in Shinar. Every generation rebuilds the tower under a new name, and Scripture's answer to it is not the abolition of nations but their conversion — the scattering at Babel answered at Pentecost, where the tongues are not merged but every man hears in his own, and answered finally by a multitude out of every kindred and tongue standing before the throne (Rev 7:9).

Hebrew 'erets (H776) — earth, land, the inhabited world and its peoples.
Hebrew puts (H6327) — to scatter, disperse; the LORD's act against the builders in Gen 11:8.
Hebrew balal (H1101) — to mingle, confound; the verb behind the name Babel.
usage: “In his days was the earth divided” — a name that dates a judgment.
“The whole earth was of one language, and of one speech” — the unity men lost by grasping at it.
The generation of the fracture is the generation of the promised line.

pos: n. pl. (the fourth-named people descended from Javan, a maritime branch of the sons of Japheth)
etymology: From Hebrew Dodanim, a plural gentilic — the name of a people, not of a single man. Some Hebrew copies read Rodanim, the letters daleth and resh being nearly identical in the older script; the KJV follows Dodanim in both places.
biblical_def: Dodanim closes the short list of Javan's descendants: “And the sons of Javan; Elishah, and Tarshish, Kittim, and Dodanim” (Gen 10:4), and the Chronicler copies it exactly (1Ch 1:7). The form is plural, as with Kittim beside it, which tells the reader that the table of nations is not tracking individuals only but the clans that came from them — the genealogy has already begun to shade into geography. All four names in Javan's column belong to the sea. They are the peoples of whom the very next verse says: “By these were the isles of the Gentiles divided in their lands; every one after his tongue, after their families, in their nations” (Gen 10:5). Nothing else is said of the Dodanim anywhere in Scripture. They are a coastland people among the far islands, holding, in the Bible's own reckoning, the outer edge of the known world. That edge matters. When Isaiah speaks of the isles that have not heard the LORD's fame and shall yet declare His glory, and when the prophets speak of the isles waiting for His law, these are the peoples in view — the ones furthest from Zion, named in Genesis before anyone had thought of going to them.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Dodanim; in sacred geography they are a people descended from Javan and settled among the isles of the Gentiles.
webster_full: DODANIM, n. plu. A people descended from Javan, the son of Japheth.
They are named with Elishah, Tarshish and Kittim, all maritime nations.
The name is a plural form, denoting a family or clan rather than a single ancestor.
Some copies read Rodanim, the letters being of like form in the ancient character.
They are reckoned among the isles of the Gentiles, divided after their tongues and nations.
scriptures: Gen 10:4
And the sons of Javan; Elishah, and Tarshish, Kittim, and Dodanim.
And the sons of Javan; Elishah, and Tarshish, Kittim, and Dodanim.
Gen 10:5
By these were the isles of the Gentiles divided in their lands; every one after his tongue, after their families, in their nations.
These are the families of the sons of Noah, after their generations, in their nations: and by these were the nations divided in the earth after the flood.
corruption_summary: A variant spelling in the Hebrew copies is offered as evidence that the text is corrupt and its history unreliable; the variation is real, trivial, and exactly the kind of thing faithful preservation looks like.
corruption_paragraphs: Dodanim is a favourite small exhibit in the case against the reliability of the Old Testament text, because some Hebrew and versional copies read Rodanim. The two Hebrew letters involved differ by the length of a stroke. The dictionary's doctrine of preservation has never claimed that no copyist ever mistook daleth for resh; it claims that God has kept His word pure in all ages so that nothing necessary to faith or life has been lost. A variant that changes one consonant in the name of an unmentioned coastal people is not a wound to that doctrine. It is a demonstration of how narrow the real margin is: the copies that differ on Dodanim agree on the ten commandments, the Servant of Isaiah 53, and every promise the church lives by.

The second corruption is subtler and belongs to the reader rather than the critic — treating the far coastlands as background scenery. The whole force of Genesis 10 is that it lists nations Israel would never meet, whose names no Israelite could locate, and that the God of Abraham is already their God by right of creation and judgment. The isles are not the end of the map; they are part of the inheritance promised to the Son: “Ask of me, and I shall give thee the heathen for thine inheritance, and the uttermost parts of the earth for thy possession” (Psa 2:8). Missions did not begin at Antioch. It began as a claim staked in a genealogy.

Hebrew 'iy (H339) — isle, coastland; the “isles of the Gentiles” of Gen 10:5.
Hebrew lashon (H3956) — tongue, language; the mark by which the families were divided.
Hebrew mishpachah (H4940) — family, clan; the plural form of the name points to this unit.
usage: “Kittim, and Dodanim” — two plural names in a list of men, where genealogy turns into geography.
“The isles of the Gentiles” — the far edge of the world, named before anyone sailed to it.
A single-consonant variant, and every doctrine untouched.

pos: n. (eldest son of Gomer and grandson of Japheth; a northern kingdom summoned by Jeremiah against Babylon)
etymology: From Hebrew 'Ashkenaz, of uncertain derivation. The Chronicler and Jeremiah spell it Ashchenaz in the KJV, the same name in a slightly different transmission; Genesis has Ashkenaz.
biblical_def: Ashkenaz is the firstborn of Gomer and so a grandson of Japheth: “And the sons of Gomer; Ashkenaz, and Riphath, and Togarmah” (Gen 10:3). He would be one more name in the northern column but for a single verse in Jeremiah that lifts him into prophecy. Announcing the fall of Babylon, the prophet calls up the armies God has appointed to execute it: “call together against her the kingdoms of Ararat, Minni, and Ashchenaz; appoint a captain against her” (Jer 51:27). Three northern kingdoms, none of them worshippers of the LORD, are summoned by name as His instruments — and they came. The doctrine in that verse is larger than the geography. God governs the pagan nations as directly as He governs Israel; He raises up the Mede against Babylon exactly as He raised Babylon against Jerusalem, and neither instrument knows whose hand it is in. Isaiah says it plainly of Cyrus: “I girded thee, though thou hast not known me” (Isa 45:5). Ashkenaz belongs to that theme. A remote descendant of Japheth, listed in a genealogy long before there was a Babylon to punish, is on file in heaven as part of the answer to the prayers of a captive people.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Ashkenaz; in sacred geography he is the eldest son of Gomer, and the head of a northern kingdom named by Jeremiah.
webster_full: ASHKENAZ, n. The first named son of Gomer, and grandson of Japheth.
His brethren were Riphath and Togarmah, heads likewise of northern nations.
Jeremiah summons the kingdom of Ashchenaz, with Ararat and Minni, against Babylon.
The spelling varies between Ashkenaz and Ashchenaz in the English text, following the Hebrew.
The nation is reckoned among the peoples of the north in the prophetic writings.
scriptures: Gen 10:3
And the sons of Gomer; Ashkenaz, and Riphath, and Togarmah.
And the sons of Gomer; Ashchenaz, and Riphath, and Togarmah.

Set ye up a standard in the land, blow the trumpet among the nations, prepare the nations against her, call together against her the kingdoms of Ararat, Minni, and Ashchenaz; appoint a captain against her; cause the horses to come up as the rough caterpillers.
Gen 10:2
The sons of Japheth; Gomer, and Magog, and Madai, and Javan, and Tubal, and Meshech, and Tiras.
corruption_summary: The name has been borrowed for a later ethnic label and then read backward into Genesis; and the summoning of pagan armies is softened into God merely permitting what men decide.
corruption_paragraphs: A medieval usage attached the name Ashkenaz to the Jewish communities of the Rhineland, and from there it became a standing ethnic term. That later borrowing tells us nothing whatever about the son of Gomer, yet it is regularly read back into Genesis 10 to construct racial genealogies for modern peoples — sometimes innocently, sometimes to serve theories that deny the ancestry of actual Jews. The dictionary rejects the whole procedure. Genesis 10 assigns nations as they stood in Moses' day; it is not a chart of modern ethnicity, and no modern people can claim or be denied its identity from a name adopted three thousand years later.

The second corruption is doctrinal and far more common. Jeremiah does not say that God foresaw the northern kingdoms would attack Babylon; he says God calls them together and appoints a captain over them. That is government, not observation. The instinct to soften it — to say God permits, allows, or works around the free choices of nations — comes from a doctrine of providence too small for the text. Scripture is unembarrassed: “The king's heart is in the hand of the LORD, as the rivers of water: he turneth it whithersoever he will” (Pro 21:1). The same sovereignty that summons Ashchenaz against Babylon delivered up the Lord Jesus “by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God” (Act 2:23), and in both cases the men who acted did what their own hearts chose and were justly answerable for it.

usage: “The kingdoms of Ararat, Minni, and Ashchenaz” — three pagan armies mustered by name.
“Appoint a captain against her” — the LORD commissions officers in armies that do not know Him.
A grandson of Japheth on file as an instrument of judgment centuries before the judgment.

pos: n. (third son of Gomer; a northern people known in the prophets as horse-traders and as allies of Gog)
etymology: From Hebrew Togarmah, of uncertain derivation, appearing also in the fuller phrase beth Togarmah, the house of Togarmah. The KJV renders that phrase literally, which preserves the sense of a clan or dynasty rather than a lone man.
biblical_def: Togarmah is the third son of Gomer, named with Ashkenaz and Riphath (Gen 10:3; 1Ch 1:6), and the only one of the three whose people are described at any length. Ezekiel places them in the market of Tyre with a specialty: “They of the house of Togarmah traded in thy fairs with horses and horsemen and mules” (Eze 27:14). Horses and mules, in the ancient world, were military goods; Togarmah supplied the cavalry of the nations. The prophet meets them again in the oracle against Gog, where they ride in from the far north with the coalition: “Gomer, and all his bands; the house of Togarmah of the north quarters, and all his bands: and many people with thee” (Eze 38:6). The picture is consistent — a hard northern people whose trade is war, gathered at the last against the people of God, and broken there. Against them stands the flat scriptural verdict on cavalry: “An horse is a vain thing for safety: neither shall he deliver any by his great strength” (Psa 33:17). The nation that sold horses to the world is finally an exhibit in the case Scripture makes against trusting them.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Togarmah; in sacred geography the house of Togarmah is a northern people descended from Gomer, noted as traders in horses.
webster_full: TOGARMAH, n. The third son of Gomer, and the nation descended from him.
Ezekiel names the house of Togarmah among the merchants of Tyre.
Their commodities were horses, horsemen and mules, the furniture of war.
They are reckoned with the bands of the north in the prophecy against Gog.
The phrase house of Togarmah denotes the family or dynasty, not a single person.
scriptures: Gen 10:3
And the sons of Gomer; Ashkenaz, and Riphath, and Togarmah.
And the sons of Gomer; Ashchenaz, and Riphath, and Togarmah.
They of the house of Togarmah traded in thy fairs with horses and horsemen and mules.
Eze 38:6
Gomer, and all his bands; the house of Togarmah of the north quarters, and all his bands: and many people with thee.
corruption_summary: Ezekiel's northern coalition is turned into a datable geopolitical forecast, and the horse trade is read as commerce rather than as the standing biblical emblem of misplaced trust.
corruption_paragraphs: Togarmah is a fixture of modern prophecy charts, assigned to whichever northern nation the chart-maker's decade requires, and the assignment is presented with a confidence the text never authorizes. The dictionary declines the game. Ezekiel names peoples his hearers knew from the table of nations; the force of the oracle is that the furthest and fiercest of them can be gathered by God as a hook in the jaw (Eze 38:4) and destroyed on the mountains of Israel to the glory of His name. Attaching each name to a current flag converts a revelation of God's sovereignty into a newspaper puzzle, and every generation that has done it has had to redraw the chart.

The quieter error is to read the horse trade as neutral background. Scripture does not. The law forbade Israel's king to multiply horses to himself (Deu 17:16), and the prophets returned to the theme whenever the nation went shopping for security: “Woe to them that go down to Egypt for help; and stay on horses, and trust in chariots” (Isa 31:1). The house of Togarmah made its living selling that temptation. The believing answer is not a lower estimate of cavalry but a higher estimate of God: “Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God” (Psa 20:7).

pos: n. (son of Eber and brother of Peleg; father of thirteen sons who peopled the Arabian south)
etymology: From Hebrew Yoqtan, connected with qaton, to be small or made little — the younger or lesser brother. The name sits opposite Peleg in the same verse, and the two together divide Eber's house.
biblical_def: Joktan is the brother of Peleg and the second son of Eber, and where Peleg's line is followed down to Abraham, Joktan's is spread out sideways. Thirteen sons are named — “And Joktan begat Almodad, and Sheleph, and Hazarmaveth, and Jerah” (Gen 10:26), on through Ophir and Havilah and Jobab (Gen 10:29) — and their settlement is fixed: “And their dwelling was from Mesha, as thou goest unto Sephar a mount of the east” (Gen 10:30). This is the southern Arabian world, the country of the spice roads and of Ophir's gold, and it is Shemite, not Japhethite. Eber's two sons are the fork in the Shemite road. One branch becomes the Hebrews and carries the covenant; the other becomes the peoples of the Arabian peninsula, listed with the same care and given no promise. The Chronicler preserves the whole list unaltered for the returned exiles (1Ch 1:20), a people with every reason to trim the record to their own line and no inclination to do it. That restraint is a mark of Scripture's honesty. The line God did not choose is written down in full, in order, with its territory named, because these men are His creatures too and the record is a record.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Joktan; in sacred history he is the son of Eber and brother of Peleg, whose thirteen sons peopled southern Arabia.
webster_full: JOKTAN, n. The second son of Eber, and brother of Peleg.
He begat thirteen sons, among whom were Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth, Ophir, Havilah and Jobab.
Their dwelling was from Mesha unto Sephar, a mount of the east.
These are reckoned among the Shemites, and are supposed to have peopled the south of Arabia.
The whole list is repeated in the first book of Chronicles without variation.
scriptures: And Joktan begat Almodad, and Sheleph, and Hazarmaveth, and Jerah,
And Ophir, and Havilah, and Jobab: all these were the sons of Joktan.
And their dwelling was from Mesha, as thou goest unto Sephar a mount of the east.
And Joktan begat Almodad, and Sheleph, and Hazarmaveth, and Jerah,
corruption_summary: Election is misread as favouritism when Scripture follows one brother and not the other; and the Arabian branch is treated as a mere aside rather than as nations God will yet call.
corruption_paragraphs: Two brothers, one father, and the narrative follows only one of them — the offence readers take at that is the offence Paul anticipated when he wrote about Jacob and Esau. The charge is that God plays favourites. The answer Scripture gives is not that the choice was earned but that the choice was free and just: “he saith to Moses, I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy” (Rom 9:15). Joktan is not condemned by being unfollowed. His house is named at length, his territory recorded, his sons preserved through the exile. What the covenant line receives is not better treatment than justice; it is mercy, and mercy that is owed is not mercy at all.

The second misreading treats the Joktanite peoples as a closed parenthesis — genealogical furniture with no future. Scripture does not leave them there. Ophir's gold comes to Solomon's temple; Sheba's queen comes to hear his wisdom and goes home confessing the LORD; and the prophets keep the Arabian south in view to the end, with Isaiah promising that the dromedaries of Midian and the flocks of Kedar shall come up with acceptance on God's altar (Isa 60:6-7). The line not chosen at Genesis 10 is not the line refused for ever. The Gentiles named in the table are the Gentiles the gospel is sent to, and the day comes when they “shall shew forth the praises of the LORD”.
